text: How should the CFO think about AI in FP&A without creating spreadsheet theater?
claudePromptBoundary: Full production prompt is reconstructed from current source template and captured source packet. ai_egress_audit stores prompt hash/snapshot refs, not raw prompt text by default.
claudeResponse:
8M and source-backed evidence status. That's a real number, but it still needs Finance attestation before it belongs in a board paper or investment case. The CFO's core risk here isn't under-investing in AI — it's investing in AI that produces outputs no one governs, attests to, or actually uses to make decisions.
That's the spreadsheet theater trap: dashboards get built, narratives get generated, and the FP&A team runs a parallel Excel process anyway because they don't trust the model or don't own it.
Three things separate real FP&A AI from theater: (1) The model output has a named owner who signs off on it — not a tool, a person. For Lakeshore, that means the CFO or Controller explicitly attesting to the liquidity forecast before it moves to the business units.
(2) The underlying data is governed before the AI touches it. The cash positioning gold table shows a quality score of 48 against an intraday SLA, sourcing from Kyriba, bank portals, SAP, and treasury spreadsheets simultaneously. That multi-source fragmentation is exactly where phantom precision enters.
AI on top of a 48-quality-score data product produces confident-sounding wrong answers. (3) Value is measured against a baseline the FP&A team agreed to before the pilot started — not after.
